Reviewer#2(Remarks totheAuthor)
This manuscript presents a compelling study on the growth of high-quality γ-InSe
single crystals under microgravity conditions aboard the China Space Station,
demonstrating that the absence of gravitational forces significantly reduces stacking
faults and activates intrinsic sliding ferroelectricity. Through atomic-resolution
imaging and piezoresponse force microscopy, the authors confirm improved crystal
uniformity and robust ferroelectric behavior without the need for doping or annealing.
Devices fabricated from microgravity-grown InSe exhibit enhanced electrical
performance, including high carrier mobility and large memory windows, while
photoluminescence measurements reveal superlinear emission with lower excitation
thresholds, indicating superior optoelectronic properties. These findings suggest that
microgravity offers a promising route for synthesizing defect-free van der Waals
semiconductors with potential applications in next-generation in-memory and
in-sensor computing technologies. However following comments should be
considered for revision before any consideration for publication.
We appreciate you very much for your highly evaluating our manuscript. Below we
willreply your comments orconcerns point-by-point.
Q1: How does the microgravity-grown InSe compare to other defect-reduction
strategies (e.g., annealing, doping) interms ofscalability and reproducibility?
Answer-1:Thank you somuch for your comments.
With the advancement of space station technology, the process of microgravity-grown
two-dimensional (2D) materials including van der Waals (vdW) layered
semiconductors becomes increasingly mature, and more and more variety of 2D
materials have been grown in space station, greatly promoting the development of
space material growth and the material growth under microgravity (actual or
simulated ones). For instance, our research group mainly focuses on the space-growth
of (doped) InSe and GeSe vdW-layered materials. As far as we know, other research
groups are successively conducting studies on space-grown GaSe, and the
thermoelectric SnSe is being considered to grow in space from the project list of the
Chinaspace station.
Taking InSe as an example, we find that the optimized post-annealing process, the
special elemental doping strategy (e.g., yttrium/Y and dysprosium/Dy) and the
microgravity-growth condition can reach the goal of defect-reduction. However, there
are someessential differences among thesestrategies.
Via post-annealing process, we have obtained high-quality InSe samples, based on
which the intrinsic sliding ferroelectricity can be evidenced from the hysteresis loops
by piezoresponse force microscope (PFM), and the intrinsic superlinear emission can
also be presented. However, to obtain cracked-free flat and large area samples by this
procedure isdifficult, although thereproducibilitycan beguaranteed.
The elemental doping (e.g., Y-doping) strategy can enhance the quality, especially the
layer rigidity of InSe with flat and straight surface, demonstrating good scalability,
although the growth process is more complicated. This product benefits for the
measurements of sliding ferroelectricity, and is also helpful for the fabrication of
high-density nanodevice arrays. However, due to the low interlayer sliding barrier, the
tiny interlayer pre-sliding naturally exists with a long layer periodicity in Y-doped
InSe, which may influence the transport performance of nanodevices, e.g., the
mobility.
For microgravity-grown InSe involved in this work, existing results demonstrate the
outstanding scalability and reproducibility, except for the special growth condition.
By now, our group have successfully grown two batches of InSe single-crystalline
ingots in China space station. Both show great reproducibility in the crystal quality
and the fundamental properties. With rapidly development of the space science
research and the in-depth understanding of the crystal growth under microgravity
condition, the scalability of space growth or microgravity-growth of crystals will be
guaranteed a lot.
It is interesting to point out that there are essential differences regarding the emission
property among the annealed, Y-doped, microgravity-grown InSe, as shown in Fig.
R2-1. In order to amplify the weak defect-related signals at low energy side, the
spectra are shown in a single (vertical) logarithm scale. The s-InSe involved in our
current work can showsuperlinear emissions ofboth intralayer and interlayer excitons.
The annealed InSe (green curve) shows excellent (superlinear) emission of intralayer
excitons (peak A) but with relatively low interlayer excitonic emission (peak B). The
Y-doped InSe(red curve) shows interlayer and interlayer excitonicemissions (peaksA
and B), but they both are rather weak as compared to that of annealed and
microgravity-grown InSe, and even weakerthan the defect-related C-band.

Answer-2:Thanks alot foryour constructivecomment.
Considering the facts that high-quality vdW InSe crystal and resulted high

growth strategy in space or on Earth with simulated microgravity environment, but
also pave up the way of in-depth understanding the fundamental physics of InSe
crystals with high-quality, push its broad applications in electric- and
photon-integrated in-memory computing chips.
We should point out that prior to this, various alloys and semiconductors such as Si,
Ge, InSb and GaAs have been successfully grown in space; see Table R2-1 from
Cryst. Res. Technol. 2018, 53, 1700265 (DOI: 10.1002/crat.201700265), and the
corresponding analyses have confirmed the significant improvement of material
quality under microgravity.The International Space Station (ISS) National Laboratory
also specifically introduce the significance and progress of crystal growth in space
(https://issnationallab.org/research-and-science/space-research-overview/research-are
as/in-space-production-applications/crystal-growth/), significantly accelerated the
rapid development ofspace material growth and research.
However, no documented researches are accessible for 2D vdW-layered
semiconductors in this realm. Generally, vdW-layered materials should have more
special advantages for growing in space, since the weak interlayer vdW forces can be
more easily manipulated by microgravity condition, e.g., to avoid the disordering of
the layer stacking sequences and even to modulate the lattice parameters.As far as we
know,besides InSe (Adv.Mater., 2025, 37, 2506506; DOI: 10.1002/adma.202506506),
other vdW semiconductors such as GeSe and SnSe are being considered to grow on
China space station. We should emphasize that the vdW InSe semiconductor
possesses high mobility, suitable bandgap, out-of-plane sliding ferroelectricity and
theoretically-predicted fractional quantum ferroelectricity (or in-plane ferroelectricity),
which is benefit for high-performance, low-consumptive photodetectors, in-sensing,
in-memory computing and even lasing nanodevices. However, the native
stacking-faults in superplastic and ultra-flexible InSe limit its practical application.
Besides the post-annealing or extrinsic doping techniques, the microgravity growth
can provideadditional strategy for improving thequality ofInSecrystals.
Thus, our work can offer a valuable reference regarding the feasibility and potential
applications of growing other vdW materials in space. In addition, the extensive and
systematic research results of space-grown InSe can provide experience and reference
formaterial growth under manually-established microgravity condition onEarth.

convection-induced crystal non-uniformity will be greatly reduced in space under the

## Paper

## Abstract

The space microgravity environment, scarcely attainable on Earth, is considered to have
a positive effect on crystal growth, especially the van der Waals layered materials with
low interlayer sliding energy barriers. Here, we investigate the structure and
optical/electrical properties of van der Waals InSe semiconductor cultivated in
microgravity environment on China space station. Atomic-level microstructure analyses
reveal that this unique environment can successfully annihilate the naturally-existing
stacking faults in flexible InSe, directly activating the intrinsic sliding ferroelectricity with
excellent retention stability. The corresponding ferroelectric semiconductor field-effect
transistors present obviously large non-volatile memory window, high on/off ratio and
excellent mobility. More essentially, they can also give superior amplified spontaneous
emission with exceptionally low excitation thresholds of photons for near infrared
nonlinear light sources. These findings not only present an unconventional strategy for
achieving high-quality van der Waals layered single crystals like InSe but also highlight
their potential for next-generation emitter-integrated computing architectures combining
memory and sensor functions.

---

## Introduction

Advancements in space technology have brought new opportunities for the development
of material science. The material growth experiments conducted in outer space since the
late 1970s heralded the birth of a new discipline—microgravity material science1-4. The
microgravity environment in space provides new degrees of freedom for material growth
and processing, while also significantly enhances our understanding of fundamental
issues related to material’s structure and property optimization5. The objectives of
microgravity material science mainly encompass three aspects6: i) preparing high-
performance materials that are unobtainable on the earth by suppressing gravitational
effects; ii) understanding physical phenomena obscured by terrestrial gravitational effects;
and iii) improving terrestrial crystal growth processes. From the improvement in one or
more indicators, the benefits of crystal growth in microgravity are confirmed with over 80%
of experiments, specifically the dislocation density in materials which has been drastically
reduced in InSb, Ge, GaAs, and CdZnTe crystals7-10 (see Supplementary Table 1).

Indium selenide (InSe), as a typical van der Waals (vdW) layered semiconductor
possessing advantages such as non-toxicity, suitable bandgap and high mobility, and in
particular sliding ferroelectricity, has attracted considerable attention11-15. As a flexible
material, InSe exhibits excellent optical properties that are effectively tunable by both
applied stress and material thickness16-19. Through optical studies, its hydrogenation and
oxidation properties have also been widely investigated20,21. When combined with other
vdW semiconductors such as GaSe, graphene or transition metal dichalcogenides, it can
generate unique interlayer excitons or form efficient type-II heterostructures22-27. Very
recently, it shows a promising potential for surpassing silicon electronics since the ~5-
centimeter wafer-level InSe single crystalline films have been successfully achieved28.
However, numerous dislocation defects29 or stacking faults naturally exist in routinely-
grown InSe crystal due to the extremely low sliding energy barrier12,30,31, limiting its
application in optoelectronic, thermoelectric and novel sliding ferroelectric nanodevices32-
35. Therefore, it is imperative to address the critical challenge of synthesizing high-quality
vdW-layered InSe single crystals. To overcome this issue, several approaches have been
successfully implemented, e.g., the post-annealing treatment31,36 or intentional doping
with the yttrium element32,33. Although they can annihilate the interlayer stacking faults
and simultaneously optimize the optical/electrical properties in γ-InSe, new questions are
unavoidably introduced31-33 including the undesirable extrinsic dopants or impurity levels
that should influence the carrier mobility, and the tuned microstructure and bandedge
electronic structure by the complicated post-annealing procedure that may reduce the
lifetime of interlayer exciton and quenching its emission.

Here, we prepare the vdW-layered γ-InSe single crystal under microgravity condition
(marked as s-InSe) on China space station. A series of physical property characterizations
demonstrates that this special strategy remarkably enhances the quality of InSe single
crystals and fully activates its intrinsic performance in electrical/optical nanodevices. The
atomic-level imaging analysis from the state-of-the-art spherical aberration-corrected
transmission electron microscopy (Cs-TEM) reveals that the microgravity condition can
effectively annihilate interlayer dislocations or stacking faults that can be frequently
observed in vdW-layered materials. It advantages the direct observation of sliding
ferroelectric hysteresis loops and the domain writing and erasing with stable retention by
piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM). The obviously large memory window and
enhanced on/off ratio in InSe-based ferroelectric semiconductor field effect transistors
(FeSFETs) as well as the superior superlinear photoluminescence with approximately one
order of magnitude lower thresholds compared to that grown on the earth (marked as e-
InSe) indicate promising applications of s-InSe in photon-integrated in-memory and in-
sensor computing chips.

## Results

Crystal growth and characterization

Fig. 1a schematically demonstrates the growth process of s-InSe and e-InSe. The ingot
growth employs the Bridgman method with a furnace temperature controlled at 715°C
and a crystal growth temperature gradient of approximately 30°C/cm (see Experimental
section). For comparison, both crystals are grown under identical parameters except for
the microgravity condition. Fig. 1b shows a macroscopic comparison between the as-
grown e-InSe and s-InSe crystal ingots. X-ray diffraction (XRD) characterizations are
performed on the upper and lower parts of the samples (Supplementary Fig. 1). The upper
part of them is the polycrystalline/mixed phase region, and the lower part is a dense single
crystal region, also consistent with the design prediction of growth conditions
(Supplementary Note 1). Notice that the polycrystalline/mixed phase region in s-InSe
features large and aggregated bubbles, sharply contrast to the multiple small bubbles in
e-InSe, because the air expelled after the solidification of the bottom region was collected
by the central rapid-cooling zone. Under microgravity conditions, this air spontaneously
coalesced into large bubbles due to liquid surface tension (Supplementary Fig. 2 and
Supplementary Note 2). Flakes cleaved from both crystal ingots present single crystalline
two-dimensional (2D) layered feature (Fig. 1c,d). XRD patterns of both crystals exhibit
similar {00l} diffraction peaks37, as shown in Fig. 1e, indicating that the single crystalline
structure of s-InSe remains unchanged in the microgravity environment. Raman results
(Fig. 1f) suggest that both InSe point to the R3m (C5 ) space group38. Notice that the
3V
A (LO) mode can be observed in both e-InSe and s-InSe, but becomes less pronounced
1g
with the flake thickness increase (Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4). Scanning electron
microscopy (SEM) images (Fig. 1g) demonstrate that the two crystals exhibit clear vdW-
layered morphology with cleavage angles of 60°/120°, consistent with their hexagonal
lattices and previous reports33. Notably, the layer structure of s-InSe appears straighter
and more uniform, which may be related to the suppression of stacking faults and the
improvements of crystal quality under microgravity. Room temperature optical
transmission spectra (Fig. 1h) show that both InSe crystal flakes (with thickness ranging
from 8 μm to 124 μm) have direct optical bandgaps with a close value of ~1.21 eV. It is
interesting to mention that they both exhibit similar thickness-dependent bandgaps even
in the micrometer scale, far beyond the routinely-accepted atomic-level thickness for 2D
vdW-layered materials. These results represent that both crystals retain various
macroscopic properties and structures of InSe with single crystal quality, except for the
potential reduction of interlayer defects or stacking faults due to the microgravity growth
condition.

Atomic-level characterization of stacking faults

The interlayer sliding barrier has been theoretically predicted to be extremely low in vdW-
layered InSe30, which can result in abundant naturally-formed stacking faults in as-
prepared crystals grown by the Bridgman method or other techniques (e.g., chemical
transport deposition) due to the factors such as the gravity, the contact stress from the
ampoule bottles and the substrate-induced non-uniformity2, as also partially
demonstrated in our previous work33. This will strongly influence the uniformity of
optical/electrical properties32,39, and may compromise the intrinsic performance of InSe
crystals. As known, the γ-InSe with a rhombohedral structure belongs to the non-
centrosymmetric space group R3m with ABCABC-stacking (Fig. 2a). It features three
armchair and three zigzag directions, and has the lattice parameters of a=b=4.00 Å and
c=25.32 Å. However, as frequently observed31, the earth-grown InSe crystals hold
amounts of stacking faults with different stacking sequences, e.g., the ABAC- ABCB-, and
ACAC-types, as schematically shown in Fig. 2b-d separately. To explore the influence of
the microgravity condition on stacking faults modulation, we perform comprehensive high
angle annular dark field- scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM)
analyses to investigate the atomic configurations of both crystals. For e-InSe, the high-
resolution TEM (HRTEM) image (Fig. 2e, with the selected area electron diffraction/SAED
pattern as the inset) together with the HAADF image (Fig. 2f) can be indexed as γ-InSe
projected along [100] zone axis with layered structures but with various stacking faults
(as similarly shown in the ref.31). The staggered arrangement between layers and straight
line-type SAED patterns can be clearly observed. While for s-InSe (Fig. 2g), the stacking
faults are obviously reduced by referring to the clear SAED diffraction spots and the
uniform HRTEM contrast32,40. The HAADF image in Fig. 2h shows the atomic
arrangement of the microgravity-grown InSe, which manifests that the s-InSe crystal
presents the better stacking-style with ABCABC sequences. More characterizations are
presented in Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6. It can be then inferred that without the effect
of gravity in a single direction, the atomic arrangement becomes more regular and the
dislocations decrease remarkably, which may significantly improve the intrinsic physical
properties of InSe crystals.

Direct observation of intrinsic sliding ferroelectricity

As reported experimentally and theoretically31,41,42, the non-centrosymmetric bulk γ-InSe
with ABCABC-stacking type may intrinsically exhibit out-of-plane (OOP) sliding
ferroelectricity, yet its observation is often obscured by the high density of stacking faults
with low sliding energy barriers. As depicted above, the microgravity condition can
effectively reduce the defects and improve the quality of InSe crystal, which may play
positive effects on the sliding ferroelectricity detection. We then perform PFM
measurements to characterize the electromechanical response of s-InSe flakes. During
PFM measurements, we have calibrated the vertical spring constant (k) and the inverse
optical lever sensitivity (InvOLS) of the probe to reduce the electrostatic contribution in
PFM measurements43. Specially, as representatively shown in Fig. 3a, stable PFM
hysteresis loops are obtained at individual points of a ~6.2 nm (~7 layers) flake with the
direct voltage (V ) sweeping from −9 V to +9 V and an alternating voltage (V ) of 0.8 V
dc ac
with a resonant frequency of ~0.5 Hz at the needle tip. The vertical electric field applied
between the probe (as the top electrode) and the bottom electrode under the sample
causes the ferroelectric-like amplitude response to show a butterfly-shape loop with an
opening of ~12 V (Fig. 3b), and the phase switches 180° at the same turning point (Fig.
3c). After cycling the tests, the amplitude hysteresis loops remain butterfly-shaped and
the phase transition remains at 180°. To exclude the possible artifacts in PFM
measurements31,33,44 and evidence the intrinsic ferroelectricity of s-InSe, we reduce the
applied DC biases gradually and repeat the tests correspondingly (Fig. 3d). As expected,
when the DC biases are lower than the coercive field, the phase hysteresis loops
completely disappear, verifying the ferroelectric feature of s-InSe. Additionally, the
polarization switching by domain writing technique can successfully manipulate the
reverse polarity domains on s-InSe flake using opposite voltages applied on the tip (as
the polarization electrode) (Fig. 3d). We also perform additional V -dependent PFM

measurements on s-InSe flakes with different thicknesses (Supplementary Fig. 8). Notice
that the piezo magnitude by the effective d seemingly presents an increase to saturation

applications in low-consumptive high-speed in-memory computing. Fig. 4a schematically

High-efficient superlinear emission of s-InSe with lower thresholds

Next, we compare the room temperature emission property of e-InSe and s-InSe samples
(Fig. 5a-d). As shown by photoluminescence (PL) spectra obtained at different positions
of single e-InSe flake (Fig. 5a), multiple emission peaks or bands can be observed with
evident position-dependence. For simplicity, we roughly divide the emission into three
bands marked by A, B and C. By referring to the theoretical and experimental reports31,
the A-band peaking at ~1.23 eV can be attributed to the intralayer bandedge exciton
emission (also referring to the intrinsic absorption spectra in Fig. 1h), and the B-band
peaking at ~1.17 eV is related to the interlayer bandedge exciton emission in InSe47. The
weak C-band, which approximately involves two separate peaks at ~0.96 eV and ~0.81
eV, is rather broad that should be (deep) defects related emissions including the
contribution from interlayer dislocations. It can be seen that the defect-related peaks are
much distinct for different positions of e-InSe, implying that there are randomly distributed
defects (Fig. 2e,f) in e-InSe. In sharp contrast, the s-InSe presents a rather simple PL
spectral shape (Fig. 5b), notably the position-independent uniformity and the narrowly-
distributed B-band relevant to the interlayer exciton emission. This may correspond to the
optimization of the interlayer stacking sequences, as evidenced in Fig. 2g,h. Fig. 5c,d
demonstrates the excitation power (density) dependent PL spectra of e-InSe and s-InSe
(in semi-logarithm scale). It is clear that the defect-related C-band in e-InSe increases
remarkably, even approaching to the level of the main A-band, with excitation power
increase. However, for s-InSe, this band is extremely weak with an ignorable increase
when the A-/B-bands increase evidently with the increase of excitation power. More
importantly, the main PL peak intensity in s-InSe is stronger by over one order of
magnitude than that in e-InSe within the similar excitation power range. These physically
reflect that the crystal quality of InSe grown under microgravity has been highly improved,
subsequently resulting in a remarkable enhancement of emission in s-InSe.

To further disclose the advantages of the microgravity, we plot the excitation power
dependent integral intensity of the emission bands (Fig. 5e,f). The integral intensity of the
defect-related C-band in e-InSe (Fig. 5e) is almost by orders of magnitude higher than
that of A-band (coupling with B-band) at low excitation powers, and then both show a
slightly superlinear increase after the threshold of ~0.8 W/cm2. We should point out that
the defect-related C-band is always stronger by one order of magnitude than the intralayer
exciton-related A-band (also the interlayer exciton-related B-band). However, the A-band
(also B-band) in s-InSe (Fig. 5f) behaves a perfect superlinear evolution with a tripled
slope (S≈3 in double-logarithmic scale) during the entire excitation power range, while the
C-band almost shows an independence of excitation power and has a lower intensity than
A-band at the high excitation power side. To exclude the influence of high excitation power,
we record excitation power-dependent PL spectra of s-InSe flakes (Supplementary Fig.
11). It can be observed that some of them exhibit a decrease in slope (or from sub-linearity
to saturation in intensity) at the high power side. However, the slope of the curve in Fig.
5f remains unchanged in the entire excitation power range, indicating that the extrinsic
factors such as the excitation power induced thermal effect can be ignorable. Fig. 5g
shows the excitation-dependent intensity ratio between A- and C-bands in both samples,
which can unveil the competition of carrier recombination between them. At the extremely
low excitation level of ~0.2 W/cm2, the main emission peak A predominates in s-InSe,
while for e-InSe the critical point is ~2 W/cm2, suggesting the much higher emission
efficient of the main peak A in s-InSe. Simultaneously, this subfigure also demonstrates
that with excitation power increase, the main A-band of s-InSe can be enhanced by one
order of magnitude than that of e-InSe, which is due to the annihilation of defects and is
much better than reports48. More essentially, the threshold for the superlinear emission in
s-InSe is reduced by almost one order of magnitude (from ~0.8 W/cm2 to <0.1 W/cm2).
This indicates that as compared to the e-InSe, the s-InSe has a higher emission efficiency
with a lower threshold that are beneficial for amplified spontaneous emission or even
lasing. Li et al.16 also displayed room-temperature in-plane lasing of vdW InSe microflake
via mechanical exfoliation. Notice that recently similar optical results have been obtained
in post-annealed InSe as-grown under gravity31, where the reason was ascribed to the
annealing-resulted elimination of stacking faults and crystal quality improvement
(Supplementary Fig. 12 and Supplementary Note 3). In view of the above results, both
post-annealing and microgravity strategies can reach the goal for improving the physical
properties of the single crystalline InSe, however, the current one is more superior by
considering the more excellent thresholds and slopes of intralayer exciton emission
accompanied with uniform interlayer exciton emission (i.e., the B-band in Fig. 5).
Furthermore, time-resolved PL (TR-PL) results in another way support this argument by
referring to the slightly shorter lifetime of carriers for spontaneous emission in e-InSe
(Supplementary Fig. 13), because the existence of more defects such as the interlayer
stacking-faults in it can trap the carriers for defect emission or non-radiation
recombination.

## Methods

Sample Preparation: Raw materials of In and Se elements (6N purity) with a mole ratio of
0.52 : 0.48 were weighted as start materials. After melting and soaking for 3 hours, the
growth of InSe crystal was started by ascending the furnace at a rate of 1.0 mm/hour and
with a temperature gradient of ~30°C/cm on the China space station and on the earth,
respectively. The specific growth process is shown in Supplementary Fig. 14. For optical
(e.g., Raman, optical transmission, PL), PFM and electrical characterizations, InSe flakes
with different thicknesses were prepared from bulk InSe single crystal via mechanical
exfoliation.

Structural Characterizations: XRD patterns of the InSe crystals were acquired on a Bruker
D8 Advance X-ray diffractometer (with a Cu target tube at 40 kV and 40 mA) with a
scanning step of 0.02o per second. SEM analyses were performed on a Zeiss Gemini 450
microscope equipped with a windowless EDS detector (Ultim Extreme, Oxford, UK).
Cross-section TEM specimens were prepared on a dual-beam focus ion beam (FIB)
system (Helios G4 UAX, FEI, USA) using Ga-ion accelerating voltages. Atomic-resolution
imaging measurements were performed on a Cs-TEM (JEOL Grand ARM300, Japan).

PFM Measurement. PFM measurements at the dual amplitude resonance tracking (DART)
mode were performed on a commercial scanning probe microscopy (SPM) system
(Asylum Research Cypher, Oxford, UK) with conductive Pt-coated silicon cantilevers. The
LithoPFM mode of the Asylum Research software was used for permanent domain writing
with the PFM tip carrying reverse DC biases (V = ±8 V).
dc

Device Preparation and Electrical Characterizations: Mechanically exfoliated 2D h-BN
and InSe flakes were transferred onto the heavily-doped Si wafer covered by 50 nm SiO
2
substrate by a PDMS stamping method. The source and drain electrode regions were
defined by photolithography and then formed by depositing Cr/Au (5 nm/35 nm) via
thermal evaporation. Electrical characterizations of FeSFETs were performed on a
Keithley 4200A-SCS semiconductor parameter analyzer matched with a vacuumed probe
station.

Optical Characterizations: Raman spectra were recorded from a μ-Raman system with a
backscattering configuration (Renishaw inVia Reflex, UK) using a 532 nm excitation
source. To avoid possible damage to the samples, the laser power was set below 1 mW
(diameter ~5 µm; fast scan in 10 seconds per curve). A Fourier transform infrared
spectrometer (Vertex 80v, Bruker) covering a wavelength range of ~0.4−15 µm was
employed for optical transmission and PL measurements. For PL measurements, the
excitation wavelengths including 405 nm and 532 nm were employed with reflectance
geometric configuration. The laser power density is set below 3 W/cm2 without excitation-
induced thermal effect on samples (Supplementary Fig. 11).

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

Jin, Sui et al. report on the growth of InSe single crystals on the China space station, and thus under different microgravity conditions to those present on Earth. The properties of the InSe crystals are compared to those of InSe grown on Earth (e-InSe), and higher quality is overall demonstrated for the space-InSe (s-InSe).
The growth of van der Waals crystals under different microgravity conditions is indeed little explored due to the technical difficulties that are implied. From this point of view, the growth on a space station reported in this work is noteworthy.
The work presented here, however, holds moderate significance to the field of 2D materials, as such a growth is difficult to be done and the proposed approach can hardly become a standard growth approach.
As for the quality comparison between e- and s-InSe, the results of Figs. 2, 3 and 5 would require a larger statistical analysis, and thus repeating the same measurements on different pieces/flakes of the crystals to ensure the general validity of the results.
The PL results are rather strange and controversial. Upon increase of the laser power, defect states typically saturate and free exciton states tend to dominate. In turn, defect states typically feature a sublinear behavior with power. Here, the authors are showing an opposite behavior, which is in contrast with what typically observed for van der Waals crystals. Furthermore, the laser powers used in this work seem to be huge. The authors are claiming that they are keeping the power below 1 mW with a spot size of 5 microns to avoid damages, but are the author sure that this power does not damage InSe? I am wondering if the strange power dependence observed in this work is actually due to the fact that the crystal is being destroyed while measuring it.
The experimental section of this manuscript is not detailed enough, especially the section related to the growth. The growth process should be discussed in detail.
The figures are not always clear. First, all figure should contain a label on top of the e-InSe and s-InSe plots to immediately distinguish them.
Fig. 1: the text in the top panels is big, while that in the bottom panels is very small and sometimes difficult to read. The Raman results are not discussed well as it is not motivated why the s-InSe shows the A1g(LO) mode while the e-InSe does not.
Fig. 5: The excitation power range in panels c-d should be specified. In panel g, the meaning of intensity ratio should be made explicit.
From the point of view of the text, the language should be checked.
From the point of view of the references, the number of works cited here is extremely low. InSe has attracted interest for a variety of reasons, including its excellent transport properties, its tunable bandgap with layer number, ferroelectricity, and so on. Techniques to modify its properties have been developed, such as strain or ion bombardments. It has also gained interest for the creation of novel heterostructures, if coupled to graphene or other 2D semiconductors such as GaSe and transition metal dichalcogenides, leading to the formation of twist-independent interlayer excitons or to efficient type-I heterostructures. The oxidation properties of InSe have also been widely investigated through optical studies, clarifying the presence of defects. All these studies show the potential interest of this material and motivate future studies. However, none of these topics and related works are cited in the manuscript. ### Reviewer 2

This manuscript presents a compelling study on the growth of high-quality γ-InSe single crystals under microgravity conditions aboard the China Space Station, demonstrating that the absence of gravitational forces significantly reduces stacking faults and activates intrinsic sliding ferroelectricity. Through atomic-resolution imaging and piezoresponse force microscopy, the authors confirm improved crystal uniformity and robust ferroelectric behavior without the need for doping or annealing. Devices fabricated from microgravity-grown InSe exhibit enhanced electrical performance, including high carrier mobility and large memory windows, while photoluminescence measurements reveal superlinear emission with lower excitation thresholds, indicating superior optoelectronic properties. These findings suggest that microgravity offers a promising route for synthesizing defect-free van der Waals semiconductors with potential applications in next-generation in-memory and in-sensor computing technologies. However following comments should be considered for revision before any consideration for publication:
1. How does the microgravity-grown InSe compare to other defect-reduction strategies (e.g., annealing, doping) in terms of scalability and reproducibility?
2. Can the authors clarify the broader implications of this work for space-based materials synthesis beyond InSe?
3. Were there any control experiments to isolate the effect of microgravity from other variables (e.g., ampoule design, thermal gradients)?
4. How many samples were grown in space vs. on Earth, and was there statistical analysis to support the claims of defect reduction and performance enhancement?
5. PFM measurements show ferroelectricity—how do the authors rule out electrostatic or electrochemical artifacts, especially in such thin flakes?
6. Authors must clearly differentiate background response from the piezo/ferroelectricity from the samples. Refer to recent publications: https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/2025/nh/d4nh00580e
7. PFM hysteresis graph appears very noisy and is taken at high applied voltage. It would be helpful to discuss possible non-piezoelectric effects in PFM signal with references.
8. How does the piezo magnitude vary with layer number of InSe? Is there any difference between e-InSe and s-InSe?
9. Authors should depict piezo response from multiple layers including bulk samples than just showing one particular layer, to confirm that s-InSe retain piezoelectricity although out.
10. The PL enhancement is attributed to defect reduction—could strain or other microgravity-induced effects also play a role?
11. Authors should consider time resolved PL and/or Pump-probe measurements to to confirm exciton lifetimes and recombination pathways in addition to providing more insights into the origin of PL dynamics.
12. The manuscript notes larger bubbles in s-InSe. Could these bubbles introduce local strain or affect electronic properties?
13. Is the observed mobility enhancement solely due to defect reduction, or could contact engineering or dielectric environment also contribute?
14. Some figures (e.g., PL spectra and band diagrams) could benefit from clearer labelling and quantitative annotations. Figure 1c-d should be labelled to improve reader understanding. All acronyms (e.g., FeSFET, PFM) should defined clearly at first use for a broad readership

Reviewer#2(Remarks totheAuthor)
This manuscript presents a compelling study on the growth of high-quality γ-InSe
single crystals under microgravity conditions aboard the China Space Station,
demonstrating that the absence of gravitational forces significantly reduces stacking
faults and activates intrinsic sliding ferroelectricity. Through atomic-resolution
imaging and piezoresponse force microscopy, the authors confirm improved crystal
uniformity and robust ferroelectric behavior without the need for doping or annealing.
Devices fabricated from microgravity-grown InSe exhibit enhanced electrical
performance, including high carrier mobility and large memory windows, while
photoluminescence measurements reveal superlinear emission with lower excitation
thresholds, indicating superior optoelectronic properties. These findings suggest that
microgravity offers a promising route for synthesizing defect-free van der Waals
semiconductors with potential applications in next-generation in-memory and
in-sensor computing technologies. However following comments should be
considered for revision before any consideration for publication.
We appreciate you very much for your highly evaluating our manuscript. Below we
willreply your comments orconcerns point-by-point.
Q1: How does the microgravity-grown InSe compare to other defect-reduction
strategies (e.g., annealing, doping) interms ofscalability and reproducibility?
Answer-1:Thank you somuch for your comments.
With the advancement of space station technology, the process of microgravity-grown
two-dimensional (2D) materials including van der Waals (vdW) layered
semiconductors becomes increasingly mature, and more and more variety of 2D
materials have been grown in space station, greatly promoting the development of
space material growth and the material growth under microgravity (actual or
simulated ones). For instance, our research group mainly focuses on the space-growth
of (doped) InSe and GeSe vdW-layered materials. As far as we know, other research
groups are successively conducting studies on space-grown GaSe, and the
thermoelectric SnSe is being considered to grow in space from the project list of the
Chinaspace station.
Taking InSe as an example, we find that the optimized post-annealing process, the
special elemental doping strategy (e.g., yttrium/Y and dysprosium/Dy) and the
microgravity-growth condition can reach the goal of defect-reduction. However, there
are someessential differences among thesestrategies.
Via post-annealing process, we have obtained high-quality InSe samples, based on
which the intrinsic sliding ferroelectricity can be evidenced from the hysteresis loops
by piezoresponse force microscope (PFM), and the intrinsic superlinear emission can
also be presented. However, to obtain cracked-free flat and large area samples by this
procedure isdifficult, although thereproducibilitycan beguaranteed.
The elemental doping (e.g., Y-doping) strategy can enhance the quality, especially the
layer rigidity of InSe with flat and straight surface, demonstrating good scalability,
although the growth process is more complicated. This product benefits for the
measurements of sliding ferroelectricity, and is also helpful for the fabrication of
high-density nanodevice arrays. However, due to the low interlayer sliding barrier, the
tiny interlayer pre-sliding naturally exists with a long layer periodicity in Y-doped
InSe, which may influence the transport performance of nanodevices, e.g., the
mobility.
For microgravity-grown InSe involved in this work, existing results demonstrate the
outstanding scalability and reproducibility, except for the special growth condition.
By now, our group have successfully grown two batches of InSe single-crystalline
ingots in China space station. Both show great reproducibility in the crystal quality
and the fundamental properties. With rapidly development of the space science
research and the in-depth understanding of the crystal growth under microgravity
condition, the scalability of space growth or microgravity-growth of crystals will be
guaranteed a lot.
It is interesting to point out that there are essential differences regarding the emission
property among the annealed, Y-doped, microgravity-grown InSe, as shown in Fig.
R2-1. In order to amplify the weak defect-related signals at low energy side, the
spectra are shown in a single (vertical) logarithm scale. The s-InSe involved in our
current work can showsuperlinear emissions ofboth intralayer and interlayer excitons.
The annealed InSe (green curve) shows excellent (superlinear) emission of intralayer
excitons (peak A) but with relatively low interlayer excitonic emission (peak B). The
Y-doped InSe(red curve) shows interlayer and interlayer excitonicemissions (peaksA
and B), but they both are rather weak as compared to that of annealed and
microgravity-grown InSe, and even weakerthan the defect-related C-band.

Considering the facts that high-quality vdW InSe crystal and resulted high

also pave up the way of in-depth understanding the fundamental physics of InSe

We should point out that prior to this, various alloys and semiconductors such as Si,

However, no documented researches are accessible for 2D vdW-layered

special advantages for growing in space, since the weak interlayer vdW forces can be
more easily manipulated by microgravity condition, e.g., to avoid the disordering of

know,besides InSe (Adv.Mater., 2025, 37, 2506506; DOI: 10.1002/adma.202506506),

possesses high mobility, suitable bandgap, out-of-plane sliding ferroelectricity and

which is benefit for high-performance, low-consumptive photodetectors, in-sensing,
in-memory computing and even lasing nanodevices. However, the native
stacking-faults in superplastic and ultra-flexible InSe limit its practical application.
Besides the post-annealing or extrinsic doping techniques, the microgravity growth
can provideadditional strategy for improving thequality ofInSecrystals.
Thus, our work can offer a valuable reference regarding the feasibility and potential

systematic research results of space-grown InSe can provide experience and reference

Q10: The PL enhancement is attributed to defect reduction—could strain or other
microgravity-induced effects also play arole?
Answer-10:Thank you forthis concern.
As known, the interlayer sliding barrier is extremely low in InSe, so there will be
abundant randomly distributed stacking-faults in the as-prepared crystals by the
Bridgman method, due to the contact stress from the ampoule bottles and buoyancy
convection-induced crystal non-uniformity, which will strongly influence the
uniformity of the optical and electrical properties of InSe. In contrast, the primary
mechanism through which the microgravity operates is "detachment growth" (a
process where crystal growth occurs detached from the container walls), which is
critical for the enhancement of the crystal quality. Under such conditions, no stress is
introduced between the container and the material. In addition, the buoyancy
convection-induced crystal non-uniformity will be greatly reduced in space under the
microgravity condition, which will also result in better crystal quality (defect
reduction).
In our work, the e-InSe used for optical property comparison are synchronously
grown on Earth following the same operation procedure under the normal gravity
condition. Thus, we can infer that the PL enhancement in s-InSe can be attributed to
theroleof microgravity.
Currently, there is a lack of comprehensive studies on 2D vdW materials. Therefore,
this work specifically explores how microgravity leads to alterations in the crystal
structure of 2D vdW materials, in turn leading to changes in their ferroelectric and
emissionproperties.

source. Fig. R2-8 shows the four PL decay curves for peaks A (intralayer) and B
(interlayer) of e-InSe and s-InSe (in a semi-logarithm scale). We can see that all
curves are similar and consist of at least two distinguishable decay processes. The fit
procedure by a double-exponential decay function gives two time constants for each
curve. As reported previously (e.g., see Nat. Commun. 2023, 14, 36; DOI:
10.1038/s41467-022-35490-0), the slow component of about 2~3 ns is related to the
carrier lifetime of spontaneous emission in InSe, including the intralayer and
interlayer excitons. However,we shouldemphasizethat our InSeincluding e-InSe and
s-InSe can give superlinear emission at a rather low excitation power density of ~1
W/cm2, less than that of TR-PL measurements. Considering the fact that the fast time
constant is almost the same for all curves, i.e., ~0.33 ns, and is by almost one order of
magnitude shorter than the slow one, we can attribute the fast process to the
superlinear (or amplified spontaneous and even lasing) emission of both intralayer
and interlayer excitons,as observed inthe steady-state PLresults.
Then, we focus on the slow time component, which is related to the spontaneous
emission process of interlayer and intralayer excitons. It is clear to see that the slow

defect emission or non-radiation recombination, compared to that of s-InSe. This in
another way can support thehigher-quality ofs-InSethan e-InSe.

Answer-12: Thank you very much for this concern. Your observation regarding the
large bubbleissueis both timely and highly meaningful.
The large bubble may represent the typical characteristic of crystal growth under
microgravity condition. As we have described in details in the response to Q4, the
schematic diagram of crystal growth process in the zone melting furnace on the China
space station are shown in Fig. 1a and Fig. R2-9a. The furnace heater comprises high
temperature zone and low temperature zone. During InSe growth in space, the
pre-synthesized InSe polycrystals is first melted in the high temperature zone for 3
hours. Then, the heater will be moved up at a very slow speed (1.0 mm/h) to ensure
the InSe single crystal growth at the low temperature zone.The specific parameters of
the resulting crystalline InSe ingot are shown in Fig. R2-9b. A total length of ~95.7
mmcan bedivided into three parts (A, B, C in Fig. R2-9)as below,
A) InSe single crystal. The controllable growth procedure ensures the good quality
of the InSe crystal in part A. In this process, the previously existed pores trapped
at the boundary of polycrystals in part A will be released and migrated upwards
(B).
B) InSe polycrystals formed during the cooling process.At this part, the raw InSe
polycrystals are heated to melt but without controllable recrystallization. So,
during the cooling process, InSe liquid in part B will transform to polycrystalline
state during naturally cooling to the ambient temperature of the space station.
Under microgravity conditions, the air rising from the bottom zone, combined
with the inherently present air in this region, spontaneously coalesces into large
bubbles due toliquidsurface tension.
C) Raw InSe polycrystals. The section from 72 mm to 95.7 mm is the region that
is not heated due to the limited travel distance of the space-based furnace.
Therefore, inthisregion, gas cannot migrateor accumulate.
In contrast, for crystals melted on the ground, gravity causes most of the gas to be
expelled to the very top of the quartz tube, so no formed large bubbles are observed.
Therefore, we can infer that the formation of the big bubble is indeed caused due to
the microgravity.Weshould emphasize that this large bubble does not introduce stress
into the single-crystal region, but it can serve as the strong evidence of the
microgravity growth process.

This manuscript presents a compelling study on the growth of high-quality γ-InSe
single crystals under microgravity conditions aboard the China Space Station,
demonstrating that the absence of gravitational forces significantly reduces stacking
faults and activates intrinsic sliding ferroelectricity. Through atomic-resolution
imaging and piezoresponse force microscopy, the authors confirm improved crystal
uniformity and robust ferroelectric behavior without the need for doping or annealing.
Devices fabricated from microgravity-grown InSe exhibit enhanced electrical
performance, including high carrier mobility and large memory windows, while
photoluminescence measurements reveal superlinear emission with lower excitation
thresholds, indicating superior optoelectronic properties. These findings suggest that
microgravity offers a promising route for synthesizing defect-free van der Waals
semiconductors with potential applications in next-generation in-memory and
in-sensor computing technologies. However following comments should be
considered for revision before any consideration for publication.

Q1: How does the microgravity-grown InSe compare to other defect-reduction
strategies (e.g., annealing, doping) interms ofscalability and reproducibility?
Answer-1:Thank you somuch for your comments.
With the advancement of space station technology, the process of microgravity-grown
two-dimensional (2D) materials including van der Waals (vdW) layered
semiconductors becomes increasingly mature, and more and more variety of 2D
materials have been grown in space station, greatly promoting the development of
space material growth and the material growth under microgravity (actual or
simulated ones). For instance, our research group mainly focuses on the space-growth
of (doped) InSe and GeSe vdW-layered materials. As far as we know, other research
groups are successively conducting studies on space-grown GaSe, and the
thermoelectric SnSe is being considered to grow in space from the project list of the
Chinaspace station.
Taking InSe as an example, we find that the optimized post-annealing process, the
special elemental doping strategy (e.g., yttrium/Y and dysprosium/Dy) and the
microgravity-growth condition can reach the goal of defect-reduction. However, there
are someessential differences among thesestrategies.
Via post-annealing process, we have obtained high-quality InSe samples, based on
which the intrinsic sliding ferroelectricity can be evidenced from the hysteresis loops
by piezoresponse force microscope (PFM), and the intrinsic superlinear emission can
also be presented. However, to obtain cracked-free flat and large area samples by this
procedure isdifficult, although thereproducibilitycan beguaranteed.
The elemental doping (e.g., Y-doping) strategy can enhance the quality, especially the
layer rigidity of InSe with flat and straight surface, demonstrating good scalability,
although the growth process is more complicated. This product benefits for the
measurements of sliding ferroelectricity, and is also helpful for the fabrication of
high-density nanodevice arrays. However, due to the low interlayer sliding barrier, the
tiny interlayer pre-sliding naturally exists with a long layer periodicity in Y-doped
InSe, which may influence the transport performance of nanodevices, e.g., the
mobility.
For microgravity-grown InSe involved in this work, existing results demonstrate the
outstanding scalability and reproducibility, except for the special growth condition.
By now, our group have successfully grown two batches of InSe single-crystalline
ingots in China space station. Both show great reproducibility in the crystal quality
and the fundamental properties. With rapidly development of the space science
research and the in-depth understanding of the crystal growth under microgravity
condition, the scalability of space growth or microgravity-growth of crystals will be
guaranteed a lot.
It is interesting to point out that there are essential differences regarding the emission
property among the annealed, Y-doped, microgravity-grown InSe, as shown in Fig.
R2-1. In order to amplify the weak defect-related signals at low energy side, the
spectra are shown in a single (vertical) logarithm scale. The s-InSe involved in our
current work can showsuperlinear emissions ofboth intralayer and interlayer excitons.
The annealed InSe (green curve) shows excellent (superlinear) emission of intralayer
excitons (peak A) but with relatively low interlayer excitonic emission (peak B). The
Y-doped InSe(red curve) shows interlayer and interlayer excitonicemissions (peaksA
and B), but they both are rather weak as compared to that of annealed and

Q10: The PL enhancement is attributed to defect reduction—could strain or other
microgravity-induced effects also play arole?
Answer-10:Thank you forthis concern.
As known, the interlayer sliding barrier is extremely low in InSe, so there will be
abundant randomly distributed stacking-faults in the as-prepared crystals by the
Bridgman method, due to the contact stress from the ampoule bottles and buoyancy
convection-induced crystal non-uniformity, which will strongly influence the
uniformity of the optical and electrical properties of InSe. In contrast, the primary
mechanism through which the microgravity operates is "detachment growth" (a
process where crystal growth occurs detached from the container walls), which is
critical for the enhancement of the crystal quality. Under such conditions, no stress is
introduced between the container and the material. In addition, the buoyancy
convection-induced crystal non-uniformity will be greatly reduced in space under the
microgravity condition, which will also result in better crystal quality (defect
reduction).
In our work, the e-InSe used for optical property comparison are synchronously
grown on Earth following the same operation procedure under the normal gravity
condition. Thus, we can infer that the PL enhancement in s-InSe can be attributed to
theroleof microgravity.
Currently, there is a lack of comprehensive studies on 2D vdW materials. Therefore,
this work specifically explores how microgravity leads to alterations in the crystal
structure of 2D vdW materials, in turn leading to changes in their ferroelectric and
emissionproperties.
Q11: Authors should consider time resolved PL and/or Pump-probe measurements to
to confirm exciton lifetimes and recombination pathways in addition to providing
moreinsights into theorigin ofPLdynamics.

Following your suggestions, we have performed time-resolved PL (TR-PL)
measurements on e-InSe and s-InSe flakes with pulsed 405 nm as the excitation
source. Fig. R2-8 shows the four PL decay curves for peaks A (intralayer) and B
(interlayer) of e-InSe and s-InSe (in a semi-logarithm scale). We can see that all
curves are similar and consist of at least two distinguishable decay processes. The fit
procedure by a double-exponential decay function gives two time constants for each
curve. As reported previously (e.g., see Nat. Commun. 2023, 14, 36; DOI:
10.1038/s41467-022-35490-0), the slow component of about 2~3 ns is related to the
carrier lifetime of spontaneous emission in InSe, including the intralayer and
interlayer excitons. However,we shouldemphasizethat our InSeincluding e-InSe and
s-InSe can give superlinear emission at a rather low excitation power density of ~1
W/cm2, less than that of TR-PL measurements. Considering the fact that the fast time
constant is almost the same for all curves, i.e., ~0.33 ns, and is by almost one order of
magnitude shorter than the slow one, we can attribute the fast process to the
superlinear (or amplified spontaneous and even lasing) emission of both intralayer
and interlayer excitons,as observed inthe steady-state PLresults.
Then, we focus on the slow time component, which is related to the spontaneous
emission process of interlayer and intralayer excitons. It is clear to see that the slow
component of both peaks A and B in e-InSe (~2.4 ns and ~2.3 ns, respectively) is
slightly shorter than that of s-InSe (~3.2 ns and ~2.9 ns, respectively). The short
lifetime of carriers for spontaneous emission in e-InSe may due to the existence of
more defects including the interlayer stacking-faults, which can trap the carrier for
defect emission or non-radiation recombination, compared to that of s-InSe. This in
another way can support thehigher-quality ofs-InSethan e-InSe.

Answer-12: Thank you very much for this concern. Your observation regarding the
large bubbleissueis both timely and highly meaningful.
The large bubble may represent the typical characteristic of crystal growth under
microgravity condition. As we have described in details in the response to Q4, the
schematic diagram of crystal growth process in the zone melting furnace on the China
space station are shown in Fig. 1a and Fig. R2-9a. The furnace heater comprises high
temperature zone and low temperature zone. During InSe growth in space, the
pre-synthesized InSe polycrystals is first melted in the high temperature zone for 3
hours. Then, the heater will be moved up at a very slow speed (1.0 mm/h) to ensure
the InSe single crystal growth at the low temperature zone.The specific parameters of
the resulting crystalline InSe ingot are shown in Fig. R2-9b. A total length of ~95.7
mmcan bedivided into three parts (A, B, C in Fig. R2-9)as below,
A) InSe single crystal. The controllable growth procedure ensures the good quality
of the InSe crystal in part A. In this process, the previously existed pores trapped
at the boundary of polycrystals in part A will be released and migrated upwards
(B).
B) InSe polycrystals formed during the cooling process.At this part, the raw InSe
polycrystals are heated to melt but without controllable recrystallization. So,
during the cooling process, InSe liquid in part B will transform to polycrystalline
state during naturally cooling to the ambient temperature of the space station.
Under microgravity conditions, the air rising from the bottom zone, combined
with the inherently present air in this region, spontaneously coalesces into large
bubbles due toliquidsurface tension.
C) Raw InSe polycrystals. The section from 72 mm to 95.7 mm is the region that
is not heated due to the limited travel distance of the space-based furnace.
Therefore, inthisregion, gas cannot migrateor accumulate.
In contrast, for crystals melted on the ground, gravity causes most of the gas to be
expelled to the very top of the quartz tube, so no formed large bubbles are observed.
Therefore, we can infer that the formation of the big bubble is indeed caused due to
the microgravity.Weshould emphasize that this large bubble does not introduce stress
into the single-crystal region, but it can serve as the strong evidence of the
microgravity growth process.

Q8: What is the main mechanism bywhich microgravity growth environment reduces
theinterlayer stacking faults?
Answer-8:Thank you very much forthis comment.
As known, the interlayer sliding barrier is extremely low in InSe, so there will be
abundant randomly distributed stacking faults in the as-prepared crystals, due to the
contact stress from the ampoule bottles and buoyancy convection-induced crystal
non-uniformity, which will strongly influence the uniformity of the optical and
electrical properties of InSe. In contrast, the primary mechanism through which the
microgravity operates is "detachment growth" (a process where crystal growth occurs
detached from the container walls), which is critical for the enhancement of the
crystal quality. Under such condition, no stress is introduced between the container
and thematerial. In addition, the buoyancy convection-induced crystal non-uniformity
will be greatly reduced in space under the microgravity condition, which will also
result in bettercrystal quality (stacking defect reduction).
In our work, the e-InSe used for optical properties comparison are synchronously
grown on Earth following the same operation procedure under the normal gravity
condition. Thus, we can infer that the optimized layer stacking-order and resulted
enhancement of superlinear PL signal in s-InSe can be attributed to the role of
microgravity.
Currently, there is a lack of comprehensive studies on 2D vdW materials. Therefore,
this work specifically explores how microgravity leads to alterations in the crystal
structure of 2D vdW materials, in turn leading to changes in their ferroelectric and
emissionproperties.
